source: recovered from hidden duplicate 18e0cf1e (Soft Toss From the Side), source framing removed
description: The base soft toss station. A partner kneels off the hitter's front shoulder, about arm's length plus a step away and slightly in front, and tosses balls underhand into the hitting zone. The hitter tracks the ball out of the tosser's hand, lets it travel to the contact point, and drives it into a net or open field. One tosser, one hitter, one bucket — this is the station everything else in the category is a variation of.
ai_coaching_notes: Toss to the same spot every time until the swing is repeatable; a station that moves the target is testing, not teaching. Tell the hitter to watch the ball leave your hand, not to guess off your arm. 'Let it travel' is the cue that fixes most of what goes wrong here — young hitters reach out and catch the ball early. Toss from a knee so your arm path stays under the hitter's eye line.
success_markers: Ball is struck out in front of the front foot, not beside it
Line drives into the middle of the net rather than pulled into the ground
Hitter finishes balanced and can hold the finish for a count
regression_notes: Move closer and toss slower, or switch to wiffle balls. If the hitter is still lunging, put the ball on a tee for a round and come back.
progression_notes: Vary the toss height and depth within the zone so the hitter has to adjust. From there, move to front toss, which puts the ball on a realistic flight path.

source: rewritten from video framing; mechanics kept from the existing description (eliminate the lower half, isolate hands and bat path)
description: Soft toss with the lower half taken out of the equation, so the hitter can only fix the swing with their hands. The hitter sets up in a wide, already-strided stance — front foot down, weight centred, no stride to take — and a partner tosses from the side as normal. Because there is no stride and no weight shift to hide behind, every mishit traces back to bat path, and that is the point of the station.
ai_coaching_notes: Set the feet wider than a game stance and tell the hitter they are not allowed to move them. 'Turn, don't slide' — the back hip rotates in place instead of drifting toward the pitcher. If the ball keeps going into the ground, the hands are casting out; cue 'knob to the ball, then release.' Keep rounds short: this is a correction station, not a volume station.
success_markers: Back foot stays planted through contact — no drift toward the tosser
Consistent line drives despite the restricted stance
Hitter can describe what their hands did on a bad swing
regression_notes: Let the hitter take a small stride if the no-stride setup collapses their balance entirely. The restriction is a teaching tool, not a rule worth losing the swing over.
progression_notes: Return to normal soft toss and see whether the bat path holds up once the lower half comes back. If it does not, the correction has not transferred yet.

source: written from the existing description (two balls, reaction time, decision making) and its advanced variation role in the soft toss family
description: The reaction and decision variant of soft toss. The tosser holds a ball in each hand, calls a colour or a number for each before the round starts, then tosses both at once — and the hitter has to pick the called one and hit it while ignoring the other. The swing is ordinary soft toss; what changes is that the hitter cannot pre-decide, which is the gap between a clean cage swing and one that survives a live pitch.
ai_coaching_notes: Use two visibly different balls — one marked, one plain — so the call is unmistakable at speed. Call the target ball as the toss leaves your hand, not before. Expect the first few rounds to look worse than normal soft toss; that is the drill working. Cue 'see it, then swing' and accept a slightly later contact point while they adjust.
success_markers: Hitter swings at the called ball more often than not by the second round
Swing quality holds up rather than turning into a lunge or a slap
No swing at all is better than a swing at the wrong ball — the hitter takes when unsure
regression_notes: Call the ball earlier, or go back to one ball with a called 'yes/no' on each toss. Younger hitters often need the decision separated from the swing before they can do both.
progression_notes: Call later, toss the two balls at slightly different heights, or make the call a take-or-swing rather than a pick. From here the hitter is ready for live front toss with a take sign.

source: written from the existing description (sunflower seeds in place of balls, hand-eye and focus) — a long-standing hitting-station variant
description: Soft toss with sunflower seeds instead of baseballs. The tosser flicks seeds underhand into the hitting zone from a few feet away and the hitter tries to hit them. A seed is small enough that only genuine ball-tracking connects with it, so the station trains the eyes without asking anything of the swing, and it is short, funny, and safe enough to use with the youngest group on a cold day indoors.
ai_coaching_notes: Stand closer than for normal soft toss — a seed does not carry. Flick them one at a time and give the hitter a moment between each. Contact rate will be low and that is fine; praise the swings where the head stayed still rather than the ones that connect. Best used as a five-minute break inside a longer hitting block, not as a station on its own.
success_markers: Head stays down and still through the swing
Hitter makes contact at least a few times in a round
Attention holds — the group is engaged rather than drifting
regression_notes: Move closer still, or switch to a larger small object such as a bottle cap or a plastic golf ball. The size is the difficulty dial.
progression_notes: Go straight back to soft toss with a real ball. The ball looks enormous afterwards, which is most of the value.

source: cues and markers written for the existing description, which already sets out the castle, the roll and the scoring
ai_coaching_notes: You stand about fifteen feet away and roll — do not throw. Roll firmly enough that the ball would reach the castle if they missed it, or the game has no stakes. Alternate sides without announcing which. The only thing worth coaching here is 'stay in front'; the low posture arrives on its own because a player defending something crouches without being told. Keep score out loud.
success_markers: Moves laterally and gets the body in front rather than reaching sideways with the glove
Stays low between rolls instead of standing up and resetting
Blocks the ball with something — glove, chest, shin — rather than letting it through

source: cues and markers written for the existing description, which already sets out the castle, the throw and the scoring
ai_coaching_notes: Put the target where the real play is — first base if you have a base, a coach with a glove if you do not. Roll from about fifteen feet, same as the base version. The cue that matters is 'field it, then find the target' in that order: the players who rush start missing both. A wild throw scores against them exactly like a ball through the castle, and saying so before the first rep is what makes them slow down.
success_markers: Fields the ball cleanly before looking up for the target
Throw arrives at the target on the fly, chest height
Gets back into fielding position before the next roll rather than watching the throw

source: written from the existing description (balance on one leg to feel fielding posture) and its base role in the fielding-position family
description: The fielding position, taught by making it impossible to fake. The player stands on one leg with the other lifted behind them, glove down in front, and holds it — the flamingo. From there you roll gentle ground balls they field while still balanced on the one leg. A player who is standing too tall or has their weight on their heels simply falls over, so the posture corrects itself without anyone being told to bend their knees.
ai_coaching_notes: Have them hold the flamingo for a count of three before the first roll so they feel where the balance lives. Roll softly and straight at them — this is a posture station, not a range station. 'Chest over your toes' is the correction when they wobble backwards. Switch legs every few reps so neither side gets skipped, and keep the whole thing under five minutes; it is tiring in a way that does not look tiring.
success_markers: Holds the one-leg position for three seconds without putting the foot down
Glove stays out in front of the body, not tucked underneath
Fields a gentle roll without losing balance
regression_notes: Let them touch the lifted toe to the ground for balance, or hold the fence with the throwing hand. The point is the chest-over-toes posture, not the circus trick.
progression_notes: Go to two feet and a normal fielding position, then add lateral movement — Protect the Castle is the natural next station once the posture holds.

source: written from the existing description and tags (cones, approach angles on ground balls)
description: A cone teaches the approach angle that words do not. Set a cone a few feet in front and to the glove side of the fielder's starting spot. Roll a ground ball toward the cone, and the fielder has to come around the outside of it — not straight at the ball — so they arrive moving through the ball at an angle rather than stopping beside it. Field, then throw to a target at first. Rotate the next fielder in after two reps.
ai_coaching_notes: The cone is the whole teaching point: 'go around it, then attack.' A fielder who cuts inside the cone has taken the straight line you are trying to break them of. Set the cone closer for a tighter angle, wider for a longer approach. Roll from about twenty feet at a pace they can handle — the angle is what is being learned, not the reaction.
success_markers: Rounds the outside of the cone rather than cutting inside it
Arrives at the ball moving forward, not stopped and waiting
Fields off the glove-side foot and steps into the throw
regression_notes: Walk them through the path with no ball first, then add a rolled ball at half pace. The footwork has to be familiar before the ball speeds it up.
progression_notes: Put a cone on each side and call which one as you roll, so the fielder picks the angle instead of knowing it. Add a time limit on the throw.

source: written from the existing description (posture and footwork, minimal equipment, anywhere)
description: Infield posture and footwork with no field and almost no equipment — a driveway, a gym, a patch of grass before the game. Players pair off about fifteen feet apart. One rolls a ground ball along the ground to the other, who fields it in proper position, makes the exchange to the throwing hand, and rolls it back. No throwing, no diamond, no fungo. The pairs alternate every rep so both are working the whole time.
ai_coaching_notes: Because the ball comes slowly, there is time to coach the parts that get skipped at game speed: glove out front, funnel to the middle, exchange in front of the chest. 'Roll it, don't throw it' needs saying to the partner every few reps. Fifteen feet is close enough that a missed ball does not become a chase, which is why this works in a car park.
success_markers: Glove reaches the ball out in front of the front foot
Ball is funnelled to the middle of the body, not caught out to the side
Exchange happens in front of the chest without the glove dropping to the hip
regression_notes: Use a tennis ball and move the pair closer. If the exchange is the problem, have them field and simply hold the ball up in throwing position rather than rolling it back.
progression_notes: Widen the gap, roll harder, and roll to either side so the fielder has to move. Once there is a field available, the same footwork goes straight into ground balls off a fungo.

source: written from the existing description and tags (shuffle footwork, fielding mechanics, communication)
description: Two fielders start about twenty feet apart facing the coach and shuffle laterally toward each other, crossing paths, before peeling back to where they started. The coach rolls a ground ball into the space between them as they cross, and one of them has to call it and field it while the other clears out. It works the lateral shuffle and forces the call at the same time, which is the pair of things that goes wrong on a ball up the middle.
ai_coaching_notes: Shuffle — do not cross the feet. The call has to be loud and it has to be early: 'ball, ball, ball' before either player commits. The one who does not call it peels behind, they do not stop and watch. Roll the ball late, as they cross, so the decision is real. If nobody calls it, roll it again and let the silence be the lesson.
success_markers: Feet shuffle rather than cross over
One player calls the ball out loud before either reaches it
The player who does not call it clears the space instead of stopping
equipment_needed: Two cones to mark the starting spots
regression_notes: Run the shuffle with no ball until the footwork is clean, then roll directly to one player and have the other practise calling 'yours'. Separating the movement from the decision makes both easier.
progression_notes: Roll harder and later, or add a third player so the call has more than one candidate. Finish with a throw to a base so the play is completed rather than abandoned.

source: rewritten from video framing; pattern and intent kept from the existing description (figure eight for range and footwork)
description: Two cones about ten feet apart, and the fielder moves in a figure eight around them — around the outside of one, back through the middle, around the outside of the other. The coach stands in front and rolls a ground ball each time the fielder comes through the middle of the eight. The pattern keeps them moving laterally and changing direction continuously, so every ball is fielded on the move rather than from a set stop.
ai_coaching_notes: Stay low through the whole pattern — the standing-up-between-reps habit is exactly what this breaks. Roll the ball as they pass through the middle, not when they are settled. 'Field it moving forward' is the cue; a fielder who stops to receive has lost the point of the drill. Two laps of the eight is a set, and three sets is plenty — it is more tiring than it looks.
success_markers: Stays in a low athletic position through the whole pattern, not just at the ball
Fields on the move without stopping to set up
Changes direction off the outside foot rather than shuffling to a halt first
regression_notes: Widen the cones and roll less often — every second pass through the middle — so there is recovery time. Walk the pattern first with no ball at all.
progression_notes: Narrow the cones, roll on every pass, or add a throw to a target after each ball. Calling the direction of the next roll as they come through makes it a reaction drill as well as a footwork one.

source: written from the existing description and the recorded flaw it fixes (slow transfer)
description: A partner drill that treats the exchange as the skill rather than an afterthought. Two players stand about twenty feet apart. One rolls a ground ball, the other fields it and makes the glove-to-hand transfer immediately, showing the ball in throwing position before rolling it back. Nothing is thrown. Every rep is a fielding rep and an exchange rep, and because there is no throw to think about, the transfer is the only thing left to get wrong.
ai_coaching_notes: The exchange happens in front of the chest, not down at the hip and not up by the ear. 'Funnel and go' — the glove brings the ball to the middle, the hand takes it there. Have them hold the throwing position for a beat so you can see the grip; a player who is fumbling for four seams will show you immediately. Count the exchanges out loud to add pressure without adding a throw.
success_markers: Ball leaves the glove and reaches throwing position in one motion
Exchange happens in front of the chest, not below the waist
Four-seam grip more often than not, without the player looking at their hand
regression_notes: Slow everything down and let them look at the grip. Getting four seams deliberately is the step before getting it fast.
progression_notes: Add the throw back instead of a roll, then put a time target on the exchange. From here the same exchange goes into the Infield Throwing Drill with footwork attached.

source: written from the existing description (fielding plus throwing, clean transfer and footwork) and the recorded flaw it fixes
description: The whole infield play, start to finish: field the ground ball, exchange, step, throw to a base. The coach rolls or hits from home plate, the fielder works from normal infield depth, and the throw goes to a player or coach with a glove at first. What separates this from ordinary ground-ball work is that the throw counts — the rep is not over when the ball is caught, it is over when it arrives on target. Rotate after two reps.
ai_coaching_notes: The footwork between the catch and the throw is the part to coach: field, right foot behind the ball, step through toward the target. 'Throw through the base, not at it' keeps them from decelerating. Stand behind the fielder where you can see whether they are throwing off a set front side or falling away. Accuracy over velocity every time at this age — a hard throw into the dugout is a worse rep than a soft one on the bag.
success_markers: Throw arrives chest-high and catchable at first
Fielder steps toward the target rather than throwing across their body
Exchange and throw happen without an extra shuffle to gather
regression_notes: Shorten the throw — field at the edge of the infield grass and throw to a coach twenty feet away. Get the footwork repeatable before adding distance.
progression_notes: Move to full depth, alternate the target base so the fielder has to decide, or add a runner to create real urgency.

source: written from the existing description (team drill, constant reps on infield fundamentals); see docs/audits/drill-canonicalization-decisions.csv for the disposition
description: A whole-team ground-ball circuit built so nobody stands still. Players line up in two or three short lines facing a coach with a bucket. The coach rolls to the front of one line, that player fields and throws to a target beside the coach, then runs to the back of the next line along. With three coaches and three lines a twelve-player team gets a ground ball every few seconds, which is the actual problem this solves: the standard infield drill gives each player four reps in twenty minutes.
ai_coaching_notes: Keep the lines short — three or four deep at most — because line length is what kills rep count. Roll the next ball before the previous player has finished their throw; the pace is the feature. Coach one thing across the whole circuit rather than correcting each player individually, or the tempo collapses. Rotate the lines so players field from different angles rather than doing forty reps of the same one.
success_markers: Every player gets a ball at least every fifteen seconds
Fielders stay in athletic position while waiting rather than standing up in line
Throws go to the target on the fly without a gather step
regression_notes: Drop to one line and one coach, and roll slower. The tempo is the point, but not at the cost of the fielding position falling apart.
progression_notes: Add a second ball in the air, vary the roll between each line, or put a team score on clean reps in a two-minute block.

source: written from the existing description (pre-practice throwing warm-up) and its existing cue 'start close, work back'
description: The throwing warm-up every practice starts with, run properly rather than as the five minutes before practice begins. Partners start about fifteen feet apart and throw easily, using full mechanics on every throw. After ten clean throws each they take three steps back, and repeat. Nobody throws hard until they have been through at least two distances. The arm is being prepared, so the reps are deliberate and the count is coached rather than left to the players.
ai_coaching_notes: Walk the line while this happens — it is the best coaching time in the whole practice, because nothing else is going on. Full mechanics at fifteen feet means a step and a follow-through, not a flick of the wrist. 'Easy arm, good feet' is what you are looking for early. Call the moves back yourself; left alone, pairs go straight to maximum distance and maximum effort.
success_markers: Steps toward the partner on every throw, even at the shortest distance
Throws arrive chest-high without the receiver moving their feet
Arm effort builds gradually — no maximum-effort throws in the first two distances
regression_notes: Stay at one distance for the whole warm-up with the youngest group. Distance is not the point; getting the arm moving with a step and a finish is.
progression_notes: Add a third and fourth distance, then finish by coming back in for a set of quick, short, accurate throws so the arm is not left at long-toss effort going into practice.

source: written from the existing description and cue (grip, step toward target, follow through)
description: Plain partner catch, treated as a skill rather than as something to do while the coach sets up. Two players stand about twenty feet apart and throw back and forth, and every single throw gets the full sequence: find a four-seam grip, point the glove at the partner, step toward them, throw, finish. It is the most-used drill in youth baseball and the one most often run without any coaching attached, which is exactly why it is worth structuring.
ai_coaching_notes: Pick one thing per round and coach only that — grip this round, the step next round, the finish after that. Trying to fix four things at once gets none of them. 'Chest height, every throw' gives the receiver something to judge. If a pair is chatting and lobbing, move them closer rather than telling them to concentrate; the shorter distance makes sloppiness visible.
success_markers: Four-seam grip more often than not, found without looking at the hand
Front foot lands pointing at the partner
Throw arrives between the partner's shoulders and waist
regression_notes: Move to ten feet and throw underhand until the catch is reliable, then go back to overhand at the same distance. Fear of the ball is the usual reason a pair cannot do this, and distance makes it worse.
progression_notes: Add distance, then put a count on it — ten clean catches in a row before anyone moves back. From here the same mechanics go into the Bullseye Challenge with a real target.

source: written from the existing description and cue (catch with the glove, cover with the throwing hand)
description: A short, single-purpose station for the habit that makes everything after it faster: catching with the glove and covering immediately with the throwing hand. Partners stand about fifteen feet apart and throw easy chest-high balls. The receiver catches and covers in one motion, then shows the ball in throwing position before throwing back. Any catch made one-handed does not count and is thrown again.
ai_coaching_notes: Make the not-counting explicit before the first throw — the habit only forms if a one-handed catch costs something. 'Catch it, cover it, show me' gives the receiver three beats they can feel. Keep the throws easy and chest-high; a ball at the ankles genuinely cannot be caught with two hands, and asking for it teaches them the rule is arbitrary.
success_markers: Throwing hand arrives at the glove as the ball does, not afterwards
Ball is shown in throwing position within a beat of the catch
No one-handed catches on balls between the shoulders and the waist
regression_notes: Toss underhand from ten feet, or use a soft training ball. The two-hand habit is easiest to build when there is no reason to flinch.
progression_notes: Throw to either side so the receiver has to move and still cover. From there the habit carries straight into the Groundball Transfer Catch and any infield work.

source: written from the existing description and the recorded flaws it fixes (slow hands, fumbling)
description: Catch-to-throw with everything else stripped out. Partners stand close — ten to twelve feet — and throw firm, chest-high balls back and forth as fast as they can while still catching cleanly. There is no step and no wind-up at this distance; the only thing that can be improved is how quickly the ball gets from the glove to the throwing hand and back out. Short rounds, because it stops being quick once the arm tires.
ai_coaching_notes: Close enough that a wind-up is impossible is the whole setup — at twelve feet the drill coaches itself. 'One motion, no pause' is the cue. Watch where the exchange happens: in front of the chest is right, down at the belt is the habit you are breaking. Thirty seconds on, thirty seconds off, three times. Any longer and the throws get wild.
success_markers: Ball leaves the glove and is released without a visible pause
Exchange happens in front of the chest rather than at the waist
Pair can complete twenty in a row without a drop
regression_notes: Slow it down and make the exchange deliberate — quality of the transfer first, speed second. A player fumbling at speed is practising fumbling.
progression_notes: Count exchanges against a clock, or make it a race between pairs. Adding a small movement before the catch turns it into game-speed infield work.

source: written from the existing description (solo throwing against a wall) and its base role in the wall-ball family
description: Throwing practice for one player and a wall. The player stands about fifteen feet from a solid wall, throws with full mechanics, fields the rebound, and throws again. Because the wall returns the ball immediately, the rhythm is continuous and a player can get more throwing reps alone in five minutes than they get in a whole team catch session. This is the base version: throw, catch the rebound, throw again.
ai_coaching_notes: Pick a spot on the wall and throw at that spot, not at the wall. The rebound comes back at roughly the height it was thrown, so a player throwing low is making their own drill harder — which is useful feedback if you point it out. 'Full mechanics every throw' needs repeating, because the temptation alone is to flick. Give them a target number rather than a time.
success_markers: Hits the same spot on the wall on most throws
Steps toward the wall on every throw rather than throwing flat-footed
Can string together twenty throws without chasing a rebound
regression_notes: Move closer and use a tennis ball, which is softer on the rebound and more forgiving indoors. Throwing underhand at the wall still builds the rhythm.
progression_notes: Move back, mark a smaller target, or field the rebound as a ground ball. The Selfies and Wall Ball Solo variants take this further with a rebounder and a rep count.

source: written from the existing description and existing cue (start at 30 feet, build out slowly, let the ball arc); safety framing consistent with the Long Toss Progression row in the same family
description: Arm strength built by throwing progressively further. Partners start at about thirty feet and throw easily. Every eight to ten clean throws they each take several steps back, until they reach the furthest distance they can throw with a good arc and no strain. This is the base version of the family — the distance ladder itself, without the structured pulldown phase that the full progression adds at the end.
ai_coaching_notes: The arc is the safety valve: at maximum distance the ball should climb and come down, not be driven flat. A player throwing flat at distance is reaching past what their arm can do. Nobody moves back until the throws at the current distance are landing well. Stop the whole thing at the first mention of soreness — this is the drill in the library most capable of hurting somebody.
success_markers: Throws carry with an arc at maximum distance rather than being thrown flat
Player uses a crow hop at the longer distances instead of throwing flat-footed
Comes back in feeling loose, with no arm soreness reported
safety_notes: Full warm-up before starting, and no long toss on a day the player has pitched. Stop immediately at any elbow or shoulder discomfort. Youth arms should not throw maximum effort at maximum distance.
regression_notes: Cap the distance well short of maximum and stay there. Distance is not the goal; throwing well at a comfortable distance is, and for most under-10 players that is sixty feet.
progression_notes: Move to the full Long Toss Progression, which adds the structured pulldown set at the end to bring accuracy back after the distance work.

source: written from the existing description (step-by-step progressions, stop over-complicating throwing mechanics)
description: A deliberately short throwing sequence for a coach who does not want to teach eight things at once. Three steps, one session: grip the ball across four seams, point the glove at the target, step and throw. Partners work at twenty feet and do a set of ten throws at each step, adding the next one without dropping the last. The value is the restraint — a young player given three cues will use them, and a young player given eight will use none.
ai_coaching_notes: Resist adding a fourth thing. If the throws are going sideways, it is almost always the step or the glove, and both are already in here. Say the three steps out loud as a group before each set so the players have the sequence themselves. When a throw goes wrong, ask which of the three they missed rather than telling them.
success_markers: Player can name the three steps without being prompted
Four-seam grip appears without the coach asking for it
Throws are noticeably straighter by the third set
regression_notes: Run one step for a whole session. Grip alone, for ten minutes, is a legitimate practice for a first-year player.
progression_notes: Once the three hold up at twenty feet, take them to the Kneel-Down Throw to isolate the arm, or out to distance where they break down first.

source: rewritten from video framing; kept the existing intent (competitive throwing game that builds accuracy and keeps young players engaged)
description: A throwing accuracy game for players too young to enjoy repetition for its own sake. Set a bucket, a cone or a folded towel out at a throwable distance and split the group into two teams. Players take turns throwing at the target, one point for a hit, and the teams alternate. The competition supplies the focus that a coach otherwise has to nag for, and the throwing reps are identical to the ones nobody wants to do.
ai_coaching_notes: Set the distance so that roughly one throw in three scores — much easier and it is boring, much harder and they stop trying. Keep the teams small so the wait between throws is short. The one thing worth coaching mid-game is 'step at it', because under competition the step is the first thing to disappear. Play to a low number and play twice.
success_markers: Players still step toward the target when the score is close
Accuracy holds or improves across rounds rather than degrading
Everybody throws roughly the same number of times
equipment_needed: Bucket, cone or towel as a target
regression_notes: Bring the target closer and make it bigger, or let each player throw twice per turn. For the youngest group, score any throw that reaches the target on the fly.
progression_notes: Shrink the target, move it back, or require the throw to arrive on the fly. Adding a fielding step before the throw turns it into a full play.

source: rewritten from video framing; kept the existing intent (flip and throw combination for middle infielders)
description: The two ways a middle infielder gets rid of the ball, practised back to back so the player learns to choose. Partners stand about fifteen feet apart. On the first rep the ball is delivered with an underhand flip — glove-hand side, firm, chest-high, no wrist flick. On the second it is a normal overhand throw. They alternate. Close to the bag it is a flip; anywhere else it is a throw, and the mistake worth drilling out is using the wrong one.
ai_coaching_notes: A flip is a push, not a toss — the arm stays stiff and the ball does not spin much. Cue 'show him the ball' so the receiver picks it up early out of the hand. Fifteen feet is about the boundary: inside that, flip; outside, throw. Ask them which one they would use before each rep rather than telling them, so the decision gets practised alongside the mechanic.
success_markers: Flip arrives chest-high and firm without arcing
Overhand throw uses a full step rather than a half-flick
Player picks the right delivery for the distance without being told
regression_notes: Drill the flip alone from ten feet until it is firm and flat. The overhand throw is already familiar; the flip is the one that needs the reps.
progression_notes: Add the footwork at the bag, then work it into Double-Play Feeds and Turns where the flip has a real destination and a time pressure.

drill_name: EASY Baseball Catch Drill — First Catch Fundamentals
source: rewritten from video framing; the two rules and the two-hand requirement are kept verbatim in substance from the existing description and cues
description: The first catching lesson, built on one rule a six-year-old can hold onto: ball above the belly button, fingers up; ball below the belly button, fingers down. A partner or coach tosses easy balls from about fifteen feet, deliberately alternating high and low, and the receiver has to set the glove correctly before the ball arrives. Both hands, every catch. Get these two positions automatic and most beginner dropped balls stop happening.
ai_coaching_notes: Call 'up' or 'down' as you release the ball for the first few rounds, then stop calling and let them read it. Set the glove BEFORE the ball arrives — a glove that turns over during the catch is the flaw being fixed. Use a soft training ball with anyone flinching; the rule cannot be learned by a player who is closing their eyes.
reps_guidance: 2 sets of 10 catches, alternating high and low
success_markers: Glove is set fingers-up or fingers-down before the ball arrives
Throwing hand covers the ball immediately on every catch
Catches balls both above and below the waist without turning the head away
regression_notes: Toss underhand from ten feet with a soft ball, and call the height every time. Split it further if needed — a whole round of high balls, then a whole round of low.
progression_notes: Stop calling the height, then throw harder, then add balls to either side. From here the same glove positions go into Over-Under, which adds the underhand flip.

drill_name: Throwing Progression for Youth Players — Knee, Hip, Full
source: rewritten from video framing; the three phases are kept exactly as the existing description and cues set them out, with the 4-seam grip and target cues recovered from hidden duplicate 28d76619
description: The whole throw, built in three phases so each piece can be fixed on its own. Phase one: both players kneel on the throwing-side knee, fifteen feet apart, and throw using only the arm and wrist — the legs cannot help. Phase two: stand with the feet wide and throw adding torso and hip rotation, still without striding. Phase three: the full throw with a step. Ten throws per phase, and nobody moves on until the phase before it looks right.
ai_coaching_notes: Each phase adds exactly one thing, and the discipline is not letting a player skip ahead because the full throw is more fun. From the knees, look for the wrist snap and backspin. Standing wide, look for the chest turning to face the target. On the full throw, look for the step going at the target and the ball coming out over the top. Fingers across four seams throughout; point the glove at the target before every throw.
success_markers: Throws with backspin from the knees rather than pushing the ball
Chest finishes facing the target in the wide-stance phase
Full throw keeps the arm action built in phases one and two rather than reverting
regression_notes: Spend the entire session in phase one. For a player whose arm action is the problem, the kneeling throw is the practice, not the warm-up to it.
progression_notes: Add distance to the full-throw phase, then take the same three phases into a pre-practice warm-up so the sequence becomes routine rather than a drill.

drill_name: Over-Under — Two Ways to Throw and Catch
source: markers and next steps written for the existing description, which already sets out the alternating overhand/underhand sequence
success_markers: Glove turns fingers-down for the flip without being reminded
Underhand flip arrives flat and firm rather than looping
Pair keeps the alternation going without stopping to think about which is next
regression_notes: Run a full round of overhand, then a full round of underhand, before alternating. Splitting the two removes the decision and leaves just the glove position.
progression_notes: Stop announcing the order and let the thrower choose, so the receiver reads the delivery rather than expecting it. Adding a step to either side makes it a genuine infield exchange.

source: description rewritten to remove the brand-led opening; the target, the distance and the scoring are unchanged
description: A throwing accuracy competition against a marked target at game-realistic distance. Set a strike-zone target, a bucket or a taped square on a fence, and have players throw at it from the distance they would actually throw in a game — shortstop to first, catcher to second, whatever fits the group. Points for hitting it. The competition supplies the intent that ordinary catch never asks for: nobody aims at a partner's chest the way they aim at a scored target.
success_markers: Player names or looks at a specific spot before throwing rather than throwing at the whole target
Accuracy holds up as the score gets close
Mechanics stay intact under competition — the step does not disappear
regression_notes: Move the target closer and make it larger, and count throws that arrive on the fly anywhere near it. A target nobody hits stops being a competition after two rounds.
progression_notes: Shrink the bullseye, extend the distance, or require a fielded ground ball before each throw so the accuracy has to survive the exchange.

drill_name: Throwing Accuracy Race — Competitive Catch Under Pressure
source: markers and next steps written for the existing description, which already sets out the ten-in-a-row race and the reset rule
success_markers: Pairs slow down rather than speed up as the count climbs
Throws stay chest-high through the pressure of a close race
A dropped ball is followed by a good throw, not a rushed one
regression_notes: Race to five instead of ten, and move the pairs closer. Resetting from nine is discouraging enough to end the drill for a young player.
progression_notes: Race to fifteen, add distance, or require that every throw also be caught with two hands to count. Alternating overhand and flip throws makes the count much harder to hold.

drill_name: Selfies Solo Rebounder — Build Reps Without a Partner
source: description rewritten to remove the brand-led opening; the rebounder setup and rep-count intent are unchanged
description: Continuous throw-catch-throw against a rebounder net or wall, with no partner needed. The player throws, the net returns the ball, they catch it and throw again without resetting. It builds the catch-and-throw rhythm that every defensive position depends on, and because it needs one player and one net it is the drill that survives contact with a family's actual week — it works in a driveway between practices.
success_markers: Strings together twenty-five throws without a drop or a chase
Grip is reset during the catch rather than after it
Mechanics at rep twenty-five look like mechanics at rep one
regression_notes: Move closer and use a tennis ball, and allow a pause between reps. The rhythm is the goal, but not at the cost of chasing the ball around the garden.
progression_notes: Move back, aim at a marked spot on the net, or put a rep target on it — fifty in a row with full mechanics is a genuine milestone for a ten-year-old.

drill_name: Clean Up Crew — Fun Fielding-to-Throw Game
source: description rewritten to remove the brand-led opening; the scattered balls, the bucket and the race are unchanged
description: Scatter ten to twenty balls across the infield, put a large bucket or a marked zone in the middle, and the players' job is to get every ball into it as fast as possible. Each ball has to be fielded and thrown in, not carried. It is a race and it looks like tidying up, and underneath it is thirty fielding-to-throw repetitions in about four minutes, which is more than most practices manage in twenty.
success_markers: Balls are thrown in rather than carried, even late in the race
Throws still arrive on the fly when players are hurrying
Every player finishes with a similar number of balls rather than one doing most of it
regression_notes: Fewer balls, a bigger target, and a shorter distance. Let the youngest players jog the ball halfway and throw from there.
progression_notes: Spread the balls wider, shrink the bucket, or split into two teams with separate buckets so there is a direct opponent.

drill_name: Foul Line Throw — First Throw Introduction for Beginners
source: description rewritten to remove the brand-led opening; the foul-line setup and the wiffle-to-baseball progression are unchanged
description: The first throwing session of a beginner's season, with the hardest part removed. Players line up along the foul line and throw out into the outfield — nobody is catching, so there is nothing to miss and nothing to be embarrassed about. Start with wiffle balls, move to tennis balls, then baseballs as confidence allows. The only thing being taught is stepping toward where the ball is going, which is the motor pattern everything else is built on.
success_markers: Front foot steps toward the outfield before the arm comes through
Arm finishes across the body rather than stopping at release
Player throws willingly and repeatedly without hesitating before each one
regression_notes: Stay on wiffle balls for the whole session, and shorten it. A beginner who throws thirty wiffle balls happily has had a better first day than one who throws six baseballs nervously.
progression_notes: Move to tennis balls, then baseballs, then add a partner at short distance. Foul Line Throw is the step before Partner Catch, not a replacement for it.

drill_name: Wall Ball Solo Drill — Partner-Free Mechanics Builder
source: description rewritten to remove the brand-led opening; the wall setup and the fifty-rep mechanics target are unchanged
description: Full throwing mechanics practised solo against a wall — the progression version of Wall Ball, where the standard is quality rather than rhythm. The player throws with a complete sequence every time, takes the rebound, resets the grip, and throws again. The target is fifty consecutive throws with mechanics that would survive a coach watching. It is the drill that separates players who improve between practices from players who only improve at them.
success_markers: Full step and follow-through on every throw, including the fiftieth
Grip is found during the catch, not after a look at the hand
Hits the same spot on the wall consistently enough that the rebound is predictable
regression_notes: Drop the target to twenty throws and use a tennis ball. Fifty with broken mechanics is worse than twenty with good ones, and the number is the thing players chase.
progression_notes: Mark a smaller target on the wall, move back, or field the rebound as a ground ball so the exchange is included in every rep.

drill_name: Quick Hands Quick Feet — Fast Transfer Drill
source: markers and next steps written for the existing description, which already sets out the short-distance pairs and the timed transfer
success_markers: Throwing hand is already moving to the glove as the ball arrives
No gather step between the catch and the release
Pair can beat their own count from the previous round
regression_notes: Slow the throws and let the exchange be deliberate. Speed built on a fumbled transfer is not speed, and at this distance the fumble is the only thing that can go wrong.
progression_notes: Time it against a clock, add a step to either side before the catch, or take it to the bag as double-play footwork where the quick transfer has a destination.

drill_name: Funnel Drill — Correct Arm Path Out of the Glove
source: description rewritten to remove the brand-led opening; the down-then-up ball path is unchanged
description: A fix for the single most common arm-path fault in youth throwing: the ball coming out of the glove sideways. The correct path funnels — as the hands separate, the ball travels DOWN toward the back hip, then arcs UP and over as the arm comes through. Partners work at short distance and throw slowly, watching each other's separation. It looks like an underhand swing that becomes an overhand throw, and it is the difference between a compact arm and a sore one.
success_markers: Ball travels down toward the hip on separation rather than out to the side
Arm path stays compact — the hand does not swing wide of the body
Player can show the funnel slowly, without a ball, on request
regression_notes: Do it with no ball at all, slowly, hands only, until the path is familiar. Then add a ball and keep the throws soft — speed hides the fault this drill exists to expose.
progression_notes: Add normal throwing speed, then distance, and check whether the path holds. Pair it with the High Five Drill if the elbow is also dropping.

drill_name: Kneel-Down Throw — Isolating Upper Body and Wrist Snap
source: description rewritten to remove the brand-led opening; the kneeling setup, distance and isolation intent are unchanged
description: Throwing with the legs taken away, so the arm has nowhere to hide. Both players kneel on their throwing-side knee, fifteen to twenty feet apart, and throw. With no stride and no push off the back leg, every bit of the throw comes from the arm, wrist and torso — which makes this the fastest way to find and fix an arm-action fault without footwork getting in the way. It is also phase one of the three-phase throwing progression.
success_markers: Ball comes out with backspin rather than wobbling or being pushed
Chest rotates to face the partner through the throw
Elbow stays at or above shoulder height at release
regression_notes: Move closer and throw softer. If the ball is not reaching from the knees, the distance is wrong, not the player — fifteen feet is already short and ten is fine.
progression_notes: Move to the wide-stance phase, adding hip rotation, then to the full throw with a stride. That is the Knee, Hip, Full progression in full.

drill_name: Point-and-Go Glove Drill — Align Your Body to the Target
source: markers and next steps written for the existing description, which already sets out the point-then-throw sequence
success_markers: Glove elbow points at the target before the arm comes through
Chest finishes facing the target rather than falling off to the side
Throws are visibly straighter within a round, without any other change
regression_notes: Have them point and hold for a count of one before throwing. Separating the point from the throw makes it obvious what the glove arm is for.
progression_notes: Remove the pause so pointing and throwing become one motion, then add a fielded ground ball beforehand so the alignment has to happen on the move.

drill_name: Extreme Catch — Progressive Distance Arm Builder
source: description rewritten to remove the brand-led opening; the step-back rule and the competition are unchanged
description: Partner catch turned into a distance competition. Every time both players catch cleanly, they each take one step back. Drop it and you stay where you are — or start again, depending on how competitive the group is. The pair that ends up furthest apart wins. It builds arm strength the way long toss does, but nobody has to be told to try, because the step back is the reward and it is immediate.
success_markers: Players use a crow hop at the longer distances rather than throwing flat-footed
Throws carry with an arc instead of being driven flat as distance grows
Pairs stop and reset rather than throwing wildly to save a step
safety_notes: This is a maximum-effort throwing drill by design. Warm up fully first, cap the distance for younger arms, and do not run it on a day a player has pitched.
regression_notes: Cap the number of steps back, or run it with tennis balls. The competition works just as well with a ceiling on distance, and the ceiling is what keeps arms safe.
progression_notes: Raise or remove the cap for older players, or require the throw to be caught above the waist to count, which stops the last few steps becoming a lob contest.

drill_name: Crow Hop — Arm Strength and Outfield Throwing
source: description rewritten to remove the brand-led opening; the hop-plant-stride-throw footwork is unchanged
description: The footwork an outfielder uses to put their whole body behind a long throw. After catching the ball the player hops onto the throwing-side foot, plants it, strides forward with the front foot, and throws — hop, plant, stride, throw. It converts a standing throw into a moving one, and for a player who has only ever thrown flat-footed it adds more distance in one session than a month of arm strength work.
success_markers: Hop lands on the throwing-side foot, not the front foot
Body is moving toward the target at release rather than stopping to throw
Throw carries noticeably further than the same player's flat-footed throw
regression_notes: Walk through hop-plant-stride with no ball, then add a short throw. The sequence is the hard part; the distance takes care of itself once the feet are right.
progression_notes: Add distance, then catch a thrown ball or a fly ball first so the hop starts from a real play rather than from a standstill.

drill_name: The Ankle Eye Drill — Footwork Foundation
source: second and third markers and next steps written for the existing description; the ankle-eye cue itself is unchanged
success_markers: Points the back-foot "ankle eye" and lands stepping right at the target
Shoulders line up on the target without the player thinking about shoulders
Throws stop drifting to the glove side within a round
regression_notes: Set the feet for them and let them feel the position before throwing. Standing still and pointing, with no ball, is a legitimate first round.
progression_notes: Add a fielded ground ball before the throw so the ankle eye has to be found on the move, then put a target on it for accuracy under a count.

drill_name: Long Toss Progression — Building Arm Strength Safely
source: description rewritten to remove the brand-led opening; the 30-foot start, the arc requirement and the pulldown phase are unchanged
description: Long toss with a structure that makes it safe for youth arms. Start at thirty feet throwing easily, and move back only when the throws at the current distance feel good and land well. At maximum distance the ball should arc, never be driven flat. The part most people skip is the end: five to ten throws walking the distance back in, which re-trains the accuracy that pure distance work costs. Distance out, accuracy back.
success_markers: Ball arcs at maximum distance rather than being thrown flat
Player completes the pulldown phase instead of finishing at maximum distance
No arm soreness reported at the end or the following day
regression_notes: Cut the maximum distance short and lengthen the pulldown. For a nine-year-old, ninety feet with a clean arc beats a hundred and fifty on the bounce.
progression_notes: Extend the ladder for older players with a coach watching, but keep the pulldown proportional — the further out they go, the more throws it takes to bring the accuracy back.

drill_name: High Five Drill — Elbow Up Arm Path Correction
source: markers and next steps written for the existing description, which already sets out the high-five position and the drop-elbow fault it fixes
success_markers: Elbow reaches shoulder height before the arm comes forward
Ball comes out over the top rather than from the side
Throws stop tailing sideways within a round
regression_notes: Have them hold the high-five position for a count before throwing, or physically place the arm once so they can feel the height. The position has to be familiar before it can be found at speed.
progression_notes: Remove the pause and let the high five become part of the arm swing, then add distance — the dropped elbow usually comes back the moment the throw gets long.

source: written from the existing description and tags (cones teaching positioning and angles on fly balls)
description: Cones mark where the fly ball is going to land, so a young outfielder can practise the route before they can read a ball off a bat. Set three or four cones out at different distances and angles from the fielder's starting spot. Call a cone, then throw or hit a fly ball to it. The fielder's job is to get to that cone and be standing still underneath the ball when it arrives, rather than drifting into it at the last moment.
ai_coaching_notes: Call the cone as the ball leaves your hand, not before — the point is reading and moving, not memorising. 'Get there and wait' is the cue: a fielder still moving when the ball arrives is the one who drops it. Watch the first step. Turning and running beats backpedalling every time, and the cone gives them a reason to turn.
success_markers: Turns and runs to the cone rather than backpedalling
Arrives set under the ball with time to spare
Catches with two hands above the head, not at the chest
regression_notes: Fewer cones, closer in, and throw rather than hit. Walking the route to each cone with no ball is a legitimate first round.
progression_notes: Add cones behind the fielder so some routes go back, stop calling the cone until after the ball is in the air, or move to live fungo where there is no cone at all.

source: written from the existing description and its existing success marker (call early and loud, the other peels off)
description: Two outfielders start about thirty feet apart and a coach hits or throws a fly ball deliberately into the gap between them. One of them has to call it — loud, early, three times — and the other has to answer and peel away. The catch itself is the easy part; what is being drilled is the half-second of decision before it, which is the half-second that produces every collision and every ball that lands between two players.
ai_coaching_notes: The call has to come before the ball reaches its highest point, or it is too late to be useful. Make the answer mandatory too — 'take it' — because a silent peel-off looks identical to a player who has not seen the ball. If nobody calls it, let the ball drop and run it again. Start with soft balls so nobody is managing fear and a decision at once.
reps_guidance: 2 sets of 8 fly balls between two outfielders
success_markers: Call comes before the ball peaks, loud enough to hear from the infield
The other player answers out loud and clears the space
No ball lands between two players across a full set
regression_notes: Throw the ball rather than hit it, closer and lower, so the flight is predictable and the only thing left to get right is the call.
progression_notes: Hit the ball further into the gap, add a third fielder, or bring an infielder in so the priority rule has to be applied as well as the call.

source: written from the existing description and cue (lacrosse stick as a target, deaden the contact)
description: A bunting target that gives immediate, unambiguous feedback. A coach holds a lacrosse stick — head up, like a catching net — a few feet in front and to one side of the plate, and the hitter bunts tosses into it. Either the ball goes in the net or it does not, so there is no argument about whether a bunt was placed well. It also forces the deadened contact a good bunt needs, because a hard bunt bounces straight back out.
ai_coaching_notes: Move the stick between reps so the hitter has to aim rather than repeat. 'Catch the ball with the bat' is the cue that produces the soft top hand — the barrel gives backwards slightly at contact instead of pushing through. Hold the stick low and near the ground; a target at chest height teaches them to pop the ball up, which is the opposite of the point.
success_markers: Ball stays in the net rather than bouncing back out
Bat angle changes to match where the stick is held
Barrel starts at the top of the strike zone and moves down to the ball
equipment_needed: Lacrosse stick or similar net target
regression_notes: Hold the stick still in one spot and toss from close range. Getting the deadened contact is the first skill; steering it is the second.
progression_notes: Move the target between first-base and third-base lanes and call the side mid-toss, which is the Deaden and Direct drill with a harder target.

source: description rewritten as instructions from the existing cues, which already set out the lane targets and the called side
description: Bunting practice where placement is scored, not just contact. Lay towels or cone lanes down the first-base and third-base lines, a few feet from the plate. A feeder tosses from short range and calls 'first' or 'third' as the ball is released, and the hitter has to deaden the ball and steer it into the called lane. Ten bunts a round, alternating. It is the drill that turns a player who can bunt into a player who can bunt somewhere.
ai_coaching_notes: Call the side late — as the ball leaves your hand — or the hitter sets the bat angle in advance and learns nothing. 'Catch it with the barrel' gives you the soft top hand that deadens the ball. The knob chases the angle, not the barrel: the hitter steers by turning the bat around the top hand, not by pushing the end of it.
reps_guidance: 3 rounds of 10 bunts, alternating target lanes
regression_notes: Call the side before the toss, or bunt from a tee into the lanes with no feeder at all. Separating the placement from the reaction makes both learnable.
progression_notes: Move to live pitching, shrink the lanes, or add a take rule so the hitter has to judge the pitch as well as place the bunt.

source: description rewritten as instructions from the existing cues, which already set out the situation cards, live pitching and scoring
description: Bunting practice with a scoreboard. Split the team in two. Each hitter draws a situation — sacrifice to third, push past the pitcher, squeeze — and gets one attempt against live pitching or a machine. Points only for a bunt that actually executes the situation drawn; a good bunt to the wrong side scores nothing. Four to six attempts each, and the losing team clears the field. Bunting is the skill most likely to be practised without pressure and then attempted under maximum pressure, which is the gap this closes.
ai_coaching_notes: The situation card is what makes this work — the hitter has to pick the bunt type themselves rather than being told. Do not coach mid-attempt; let the failed ones fail and talk afterwards. Live pitching matters here more than anywhere else in the bunting category, because bunting a machine ball is a different skill from bunting a teammate's.
regression_notes: Drop to one bunt type per round and toss instead of pitching. The competition still works, and the decision can be added once the technique holds up.
progression_notes: Add a runner so the bunt has a real consequence, tighten the target areas, or make an unexecuted bunt cost a point rather than simply scoring none.

drill_name: Call It Early — Outfield Communication Basics
source: description rewritten as instructions from the existing cues, which already set out the pre-peak call rule and the verbal answer
description: The introduction to calling the ball, with one rule that makes it teachable: the call has to come before the ball reaches its highest point, and it has to be said three times. Two fielders, one coach tossing high balls into the space between them. One calls 'mine, mine, mine', the other answers 'take it, take it' and peels away. Soft balls to start, so nobody is deciding and flinching at the same time.
ai_coaching_notes: Before the peak is the rule, because after the peak there is no time for the other player to react. Three times is not arbitrary either — once is easy to miss under a helmet in wind. Make the answer compulsory; that is the half of it most coaches skip, and it is the half that prevents the collision.
regression_notes: Toss lower and slower, or have the players call the ball with no catch at all — just the call and the peel. The verbal habit can be built before the catching is reliable.
progression_notes: Toss higher and further into the gap, then move to live fungo. Adding an infielder turns it into the priority drill, where the call also has to be overruled correctly.

source: description rewritten as instructions from the existing cues, which already set out the tweener balls and the freeze-and-ask method
description: The ball hit between the infield and the outfield — the tweener — and the rule about who takes it. Position an infielder and an outfielder in the same lane and hit balls deliberately into the space between them. The rule is plain: the outfielder is coming in and can see the whole play, so any ball they call is theirs, and the infielder yields. Freeze the play after every rep and ask the group whose ball it was and why.
ai_coaching_notes: The freeze-and-ask is the teaching, not the reps. Players who can state the rule out loud apply it in a game; players who have only been shouted at during one do not. Hit the genuinely awkward ones on purpose — the easy tweeners teach nothing. Watch that the infielder peels out of the landing zone rather than stopping in it.
regression_notes: Throw rather than hit, and tell them the answer before the rep so the movement can be practised without the decision.
progression_notes: Add a second infielder, or run it live within a team defence period where the priority has to survive everything else going on.

source: description rewritten as instructions from the existing cues, which already set out the anchor height, light tension and pre-throwing placement
description: The band routine that happens before anyone picks up a ball. Anchor the bands to a fence at about elbow height and work through the standard shoulder set — external rotation, internal rotation, reverse throw, forward throw — eight to ten light reps of each. The resistance should be enough to feel and not enough to strain. It takes five minutes, it goes first, every time, and it is the cheapest arm insurance in youth baseball.
ai_coaching_notes: Anchor at elbow height and keep the tension light — these are activation reps, not strength reps. 'Slow out, slow back', with no snap at the end of the band. The habit is the hard part, not the exercises: make it the first station on the field rather than something offered to players who arrive early.
regression_notes: Fewer exercises and lighter bands, or no band at all — arm circles and slow reach-throughs activate the same area for a first-year player.
progression_notes: Move to the nine-exercise strength routine on low-throwing days. The activation version stays as the pre-throwing routine regardless; the strength version is additional, not a replacement.

source: description rewritten as instructions from the existing cues, which already set out the 15-minute window and the light-and-rhythmic standard
description: What a pitcher does in the fifteen minutes after their last pitch. Eight light exercises — band work through the shoulder, slow arm circles, reach-throughs, gentle range-of-motion work — done at an effort that feels easier than the warm-up did. Nothing here is strength work. The purpose is to move blood through an arm that has just been asked for a lot, and the only thing that makes it effective is doing it every outing rather than the ones where the arm already aches.
ai_coaching_notes: Fifteen minutes is the window, and consistency is the entire mechanism — a recovery routine done half the time does roughly nothing. Keep it light and rhythmic. Get players to note next-day soreness for a couple of weeks; seeing their own numbers change is what makes a twelve-year-old keep doing it.
reps_guidance: 1 round of 8 exercises immediately after throwing
regression_notes: Four exercises done every time beats eight done occasionally. Cut the list before you cut the frequency.
progression_notes: Pair it with the pre-throwing activation routine so the arm is bracketed at both ends, and add next-day mobility work for players throwing on consecutive days.

source: description rewritten as instructions from the existing cues, which already set out the tempo, the low-throwing-day placement and the elbow-height check
description: A standalone band workout for the rotator cuff and the muscles around the shoulder blade, run on days with little or no throwing. Nine exercises, two sets of ten, at a controlled two-second tempo in each direction. Unlike the pre-throwing activation routine this is genuine strength work and it belongs on a light day — doing it after a max-effort outing takes away the recovery it is meant to support.
ai_coaching_notes: Two seconds out, two seconds back, on every rep — speed is how players make band work useless. Elbows stay at the height you set them; an elbow drifting down is a fatigue signal and the cue to stop the set rather than push through it. Progress the band colour only after three or four weeks at a clean tempo.
regression_notes: Cut to five exercises and one set, with the lightest band available. Tempo and control matter more than the exercise count at every age in this library.
progression_notes: Add resistance rather than reps, and keep the tempo. Once this is routine, the pre-throwing activation routine can be shortened because the baseline strength is there.

drill_name: Complete Pitching and Throwing Warm-Up Routine
source: description rewritten as instructions from the existing cues, which already set out the big-to-small arm circles and the progressive throwing sequence
description: The full pre-throwing sequence, in order: move the whole body first, then the shoulder, then the arm with a ball. Jog and do dynamic leg movements, then large arm circles becoming progressively smaller, then band or reach-through shoulder work, then throw — starting close and easy, building distance and effort gradually. It takes about ten minutes and it is the same routine before a practice and before a game, which is most of why it works.
ai_coaching_notes: Whole body before arm, every time — a warm shoulder on a cold body is not a warm-up. Big circles to small is the sequence players remember. The progressive throwing at the end is part of the routine, not the practice that follows it: nobody throws hard until they have thrown easy first. Tell them out loud that reporting a sore arm is what you want, not something to avoid.
regression_notes: Shorten the throwing ladder and keep the movement work. For the youngest groups, five minutes of moving and two distances of easy throwing is a complete warm-up.
progression_notes: Add the band activation routine before the throwing phase, and extend the throwing ladder for pitchers who are about to throw a bullpen.

drill_name: Baseball Arm Stretches and Pre-Throwing Warm-Up
source: rewritten from video framing; the arm circles, gentle-stretch standard and never-throw-cold rule are kept from the existing description and cues
description: A five-minute arm and shoulder preparation done before a ball is picked up. Arm circles forward and backward, starting large and getting smaller. Cross-body shoulder stretches held gently. Reach-throughs and slow trunk rotations. No equipment, no partner, and it works on a touchline or in a car park. It is the shortest routine in the library and it is the one that should never be skipped, because throwing cold is how youth arms get hurt.
ai_coaching_notes: Gentle pull, never pain — a stretch that hurts is doing the opposite of what it is for. Slow and controlled beats big range. Do it as a group so it takes the same five minutes for everyone and nobody is negotiating. 'Warm up to throw, do not throw to warm up' is worth saying out loud until the players say it back.
success_markers: Full pain-free range of motion in both shoulders before throwing
Players start the routine without being told
Nobody picks up a ball before the routine is finished
regression_notes: Three movements instead of six, done properly. A short routine that happens is worth more than a complete one that gets skipped when practice starts late.
progression_notes: Add band activation for players who throw a lot, and extend into the full pre-throwing warm-up on game days.

drill_name: Baseball Dynamic Stretches for Youth Players
source: description rewritten as instructions from the existing cues, which already set out the smooth-and-controlled standard and the gentle-pull limit
description: A moving warm-up built around the positions baseball actually asks for: leg swings forward and sideways, walking lunges with a trunk rotation, arm swings across the body, hip openers, and slow trunk twists. Everything is done moving rather than held, over about fifteen yards each. It raises temperature and range of motion at the same time, which is what a warm-up is for — a static stretch on a cold body does neither.
ai_coaching_notes: Smooth and controlled, not big and fast — the range comes from repetition, not from forcing it. A gentle pull is the limit. Run it as a group moving down a line so everyone does the same movement at the same time, which is the only practical way to keep twelve eight-year-olds stretching. Anything that hurts is a stop-and-tell-me, not a push-through.
success_markers: Players move through the full range without forcing or bouncing
Group completes the sequence together rather than drifting
Nobody reports pain during the routine
regression_notes: Fewer movements over a shorter distance. Four done well is a warm-up; ten done badly is a queue.
progression_notes: Add the arm-specific stretches and band activation before throwing days, and lengthen the distance for older players who need more cardiovascular preparation.

source: next steps written for the existing description, which already sets out the charge, the glove-side pickup and the throw home
regression_notes: Roll the ball rather than hitting it, and shorten the throw to second base. The charging footwork is the skill; the distance to the plate is what makes it a max-effort throw, and that can wait.
progression_notes: Hit the ball harder and to either side, add a live runner so the decision to go do-or-die is real, and chart the time from pickup to catch at the plate.

source: description rewritten to remove the brand-led opening; markers and next steps written for the existing cues
description: The first movement an outfielder makes on a ball hit over their head. Instead of backpedalling, the fielder drops the foot on the ball's side straight back, opens the hips, turns, and runs. The coach stands in front, points or throws to one side, and the fielder drop steps and runs to the spot. Both sides, every session. It is the most fundamental outfield movement there is, and backpedalling — which is what every untaught player does — is both slower and how outfielders fall over.
ai_coaching_notes: Drop the foot back, do not step across — a crossover first step turns the hips the wrong way. 'Open the gate' is the cue that gets the hip to rotate. Run to the spot and then find the ball; players who try to watch the ball the whole way end up drifting. Practise both sides deliberately, because everyone has a strong one and a side they avoid.
success_markers: First step goes back and opens the hips rather than backpedalling
Turns and runs, then locates the ball, rather than tracking it the whole way
Drop steps to the weaker side look like the stronger side by the end of a session
regression_notes: Point rather than throw, and let them drop step and run to a cone with no ball at all. The footwork is learnable before the catch is.
progression_notes: Throw the ball as they turn so they have to find it mid-run, then move to live fungo where they read it off the bat.

source: markers and next steps written for the existing description, which already sets out the active upper-body sequence and the gentle-pull limit
success_markers: Shoulders move through full range without forcing
Routine is finished before anyone picks up a ball
Players can run the sequence themselves by mid-season
regression_notes: Cut to the three arm movements and skip the rest. Something short that happens every time beats a full routine that gets dropped when practice starts late.
progression_notes: Add band activation before throwing days, and follow with a progressive throwing ladder rather than going straight to full-distance catch.

drill_name: 8 Baseball Warm-Up Exercises You Must Do
source: markers and next steps written for the existing description, which already sets out the eight exercises and the 15-20 yard distance
success_markers: Chest stays up and the movement stays controlled across all eight
Group finishes together rather than strung out
Easy throws at the end look like proper throws, not flicks
regression_notes: Pick four of the eight and shorten to ten yards. The sequence matters less than the fact that the body is moving before the balls come out.
progression_notes: Extend the distance, add a change-of-direction element to the shuffles and backpedals, and lengthen the progressive throwing at the end on game days.

source: description rewritten to remove the brand-led opening; markers and next steps written for the existing cues
description: A timed circuit around the bases that trains acceleration, turning and body control rather than baserunning rules. Players run the full circuit — home to first with a turn, first to third, third to home — hitting the inside corner of each base and staying low through the turns. Time each round and let them chase their own number. It develops the sprint mechanics and change of direction that every part of the game depends on, in a format a nine-year-old will do repeatedly without being asked twice.
ai_coaching_notes: Hit the inside corner of the base and lean into the turn — a player who runs wide and pops up tall loses more time at the bag than they gain on the straight. Arms pump; they do not flail. Time every round out loud so there is a number to beat. Two or three rounds is plenty, with real rest between; this is a speed drill and a tired sprint trains the wrong thing.
success_markers: Touches the inside corner of each base
Stays low through the turn instead of standing up
Round times improve or hold across the session rather than degrading
regression_notes: Run half the circuit — home to second — and drop the clock. The turn mechanics are the skill; the full lap is just conditioning.
progression_notes: Add a lead and a start signal, or run two players staggered so there is someone to chase. Timing the segments separately shows which turn is costing them.

source: written from the existing description and cue (tee out in front, line drives to the middle); base of the tee-work family
description: The base hitting station and the one every other hitting drill assumes. A ball on a tee, set at belt height and positioned just in front of the hitter's front foot, and the hitter swings. Because the ball does not move, nothing about timing can go wrong, which leaves the swing itself as the only variable. Three sets of ten, into a net or out onto a field, with the coach watching one thing at a time.
ai_coaching_notes: Tee placement is the coaching. In front of the front foot produces extension; too deep produces the weak ground ball to second that half a youth lineup hits every week. Coach one thing per set and say what you are watching for before it starts. A ball that leaves with a snap rather than a thud is the audible version of good contact, and players can hear their own.
success_markers: Hits firm line drives back up the middle, not pop-ups or choppers
Contact happens in front of the front foot
Finishes balanced enough to hold the finish for a count
regression_notes: Lower the tee and move it closer to the middle of the stance, and use a larger ball. A hitter missing the tee itself needs an easier target before they need a better swing.
progression_notes: Move the tee further forward for extension work, or higher and lower for the High Tee and Low Tee variations. Soft toss is the next step once the swing repeats off a still ball.

source: recovered from hidden duplicate 874e0c3a (High Tee Drill), whose description and cues were richer than this canonical row's; base of the high-tee family
description: The tee set at the top of the strike zone, around chest height, for the pitch most young hitters get under. A high pitch needs a short, flat path — the hitter's hands stay above the ball and the barrel matches the plane of the pitch rather than swinging up at it. It is the direct fix for the hitter who drops their hands on every swing and pops up anything above the belt.
ai_coaching_notes: Hands above the ball is the whole cue, and it is worth saying before every set because the habit is strong. Watch for the barrel dragging behind the hands — if it does, the hands are not moving fast enough, not that the swing is too short. A backspun line drive toward second base is the shape you want; a high fly ball means they got underneath it again.
success_markers: Hands stay above the ball through contact
Line drives with backspin rather than high fly balls
Swing stays short — no loop on its way to a chest-high ball
regression_notes: Drop the tee to belt height until the path is repeatable, then raise it back gradually. A hitter who cannot square up a belt-high ball is not ready to be fixed at the letters.
progression_notes: Alternate between the high tee and the low tee within a round so the hitter has to adjust the path, or move to front toss up in the zone.

source: written from the existing description, cue and success marker (stay in the legs, drive low pitches on a line)
description: The tee set low, around knee height, for the pitch that produces most of the weak contact in youth baseball. The low pitch is where hitters either stay down in their legs and drive it, or stand up, drop the barrel underneath it, and pop it straight up. Setting the tee down there makes the difference obvious immediately, because the two swings produce completely different ball flights.
ai_coaching_notes: 'Stay in your legs' is the cue, and the failure it prevents is standing up — a hitter who straightens their back leg to reach a low ball has lost the swing before contact. Bend from the knees, not the waist. A popped-up ball off a low tee means the barrel got underneath it; a hard ground ball means they came over the top. The line drive is between the two.
success_markers: Stays in the legs and drives low pitches on a line, not under them
Back knee stays bent through contact rather than straightening
No pop-ups across a full set
